features.name: Ephyra
features.note: (Corinth)

features.name: Orchomenos
features.note:
Founded by Minyas, son of Aiolos

there's a story that Minyas

set out thence—Minyas, Aiolos's son—and founded

Orchómenos, that city that marches with the Kadmeians.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 3.1093–1095, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Pytho
features.note: (Delphoi)

features.name: Pagasai
features.note:
The starting point for Jason's journey.

Now when he got beyond the city's well-built streets,

and reached the headland of Págasai, where his companions

were awaiting him, assembled beside Argo, their vessel,

he stood at the harbor's edge, and they gathered before him.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.317–320, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Kyzikos City
features.note:
Within the Propontis there stands a beetling island,

just offshore from the fertile Phrygian domain,

sloping down to the sea, with sea-washed isthmus,

and sheer on the landward side. Its shores possess double

promontories. It lies north of the Aísepos River, 

and dwellers round about call it Bear Mountain.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.936–941, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Fair Haven
features.note:
Hither Argo sailed onward, sped by Thracian winds,

and the Fair Haven welcomed her as she ran before them.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.953–954, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Meliboia
features.note:
From there they continued their voyage, passing Meliboia, 

seeing its craggy heights, its gale-swept shoreline.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.592–593, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Homólé
features.note:
As dawn came up, they sighted Homólé, lying

flush with the sea, and sailed past it: not long after

they skirted the outflow of the Amyros estuary.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.594–596, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Rhoiteion
features.note:
They left the open sea behind them

at dawn and by nightfall were steering under the lee of

Rhoiteion's headland, with Ida firm on their starboard bow.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.927–929, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Dardania
features.note:
Leaving Dardania, they set course for Abydos,

passing Perkóté next, and Abámis's sandy strand,

and sacred Pityeia.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.930–932, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Abydos
features.note:
Leaving Dardania, they set course for Abydos,

passing Perkóté next, and Abámis's sandy strand,

and sacred Pityeia.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.930–932, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Perkóté
features.note:
Leaving Dardania, they set course for Abydos,

passing Perkóté next, and Abámis's sandy strand,

and sacred Pityeia.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.930–932, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Abámis
features.note:
Leaving Dardania, they set course for Abydos,

passing Perkóté next, and Abámis's sandy strand,

and sacred Pityeia.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.930–932, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Pityeia
features.note:
Leaving Dardania, they set course for Abydos,

passing Perkóté next, and Abámis's sandy strand,

and sacred Pityeia.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.930–932, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Kios
features.note:
At the hour when a ploughman or gardener, much relieved,

gets home to his cottage, ravenous for supper,

and on the threshold, knees buckling with exhaustion,

sunburnt, dust-caked, contemplates his toil-worn

hands, and calls down many curses on his belly:

then was the time they reached the habitations of Kios

by Mount Arganthónios and the Kios River's outfall. [1172–1178]

features.name: Outpost of Amykos
features.note: The Bithynian territory is NE of this outpost, however the Bithynians have continued to push their territory east.

features.name: Pimpleia
features.note:
First in our record be Orpheus, whom famous Kallíope,

after bedding Thracian Oiágros, bore, they tell us,

hard by Pimpleia's high rocky lookout: Orpheus,

who's said to have charmed unshiftable upland boulders

and the flow of rivers with the sound of his music.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.23–27, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Peiresiai
features.note:
Soon, too came Asteríon, begotten of Kométes

by Apídanos' turbulent waters, who had his dwelling

in Peirésiai of Thessalia, under a lofty mountain,

where mighty Apídanos and divine Enípeus

have their juncture, uniting in one from remote beginnings. [35–39]

features.name: Lárissa
features.note:
After them, leaving Lárissa, there followed that Polyphémos,

Eílatos's son, who once, among the sturdy Lapiths,

when the Lapiths were arming themselves against the Centaurs,

fought as a youth; though now his limbs were heavy

with age, his spirit remained a warrior's as always.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.40–44, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Myrína
features.note:
[...] Though its distance from Lemnos

is as much as a well-found merchantman sails in a morning,

yet its highest peak casts a shadow as far as Myrína.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.602–604, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: 3. Banquet with the Lemnians
features.note:
Jason and his companions meet the Lemnians who convince them to stay and banquet with them, which they do for days.

“Stranger, why have you all sat waiting so long like this

outside our towers? 

[...]

So do you abide among us! If it be your pleasure

to choose to settle here, then the perquisites and honors

of my father, Thóas, would all be yours; 

[...]

“Hypsípylé, most gladly would we accept your welcome

offer, which matches so well with our own desires.

[...] But the monarchy and the island—

these must be your own care.

After some time, Herakles—who stayed behind—chides them to embark again.

“You wretched creatures, is it murder of kin that keeps us

far from our country? Was it for lack of weddings

that we came thence hither, scorning our native ladies?

Is it our pleasure to dwell here, sharing out rich Lemnian lots?

We'll not win renown cooped up for all this time

with a passel of foreign women,

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.793–840 & 1.865–870, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: 1. The voyage begins
features.note:
Jason and his companions embark on their voyage from the Pagasaian headlands.

But when radiant dawn looked out with eyes of brightness

on the high peaks of Pelion, and the morning

breeze stirred the sea, left the headlands calm and clear,

then Tiphys arose, and roused up his companions

to board the ship, and set their oars for rowing.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.519–523, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: 5. King Kyzikós and the Doliónes
features.note:
Jason and the Minyans meet King Kyzikós and the Doliónes, who greet them in friendship. They are then invited to move their ship to the city harbor. 

All together, the Doliónes, and Kyzikós in person,

came out to meet them in friendship, after they'd ascertained

what their race was, and why this voyage; hailed them hospitably,

issued an invitation to row on further, cast their

mooring hawsers ashore inside the city harbor. 

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.961–965, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: 7. Battle of the Dolionés
features.note:
The argo is forced by weather to return to Kyzikós at night and a battle ensues. King Kyzikós dies and the Argonauts mourn him along with the Dolionés.

The ship ran all day under canvas; but at nightfall

the steady breeze dropped, and a contrary hurricane

whirled them about and drove them right back once more

to their kind hosts the Doliónes.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.1015–1018, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: 2. Tomb of Dolops
features.note:
The argonauts stop at the tomb of Dolops.

[...] and the tomb of Dolops. There, towards evening,

they were driven by contrary winds to beach their vessel,

and at dusk, as a swell got up, in Dolops's honor

they burnt joints of sheep for the dead.

 

They linger for two days and then depart. The beach Aphétai, "the departure point", get's its name from this.

Two days they lingered

idle upon the shore there, but on the third refloated

their vessel, hauling aloft its ample canvas: men still

refer to that beach as Aphétai, the “departure point” of Argo.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.585–591, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: 4. Samothrakian Mysteries
features.note:
The argonauts were initiated in the Samothrakian mysteries, the evening after leaving Lemnos.

Towards evening, at Orpheus's behest, they beached their vessel

on the island of Atlas's daughter Elektra, that by learning

those secret rites, with their benign initiations,

they might steer in greater safety across the chilling deep.

Of such rites I say no more, but bid farewell to

the island itself and its indwelling deities, whose

are the mystery cults, which here we may not mention.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.915–921, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: 6. Battle of the Aborigines
features.note:
After the guesting with the Doliónes, some of the Argonauts are attacked while moving their boat by the aborigines.

But the aborigines, charging around the mountain,

with showers of rocks to the bottom began to dam     

Bar Harbor mouth, as though trapping a sea beast inside.

[...]

Soon the rest joined him, hurrying back before they'd

scaled the lookout peak, true warrior heroes,

and slaughtered the aborigines, repelling

their charges with arrows and spear thrusts, till they'd brought down

every last one of these stubborn, frenzied attackers.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.989–1002, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: 8. Altar to Rhea
features.note:
After being stranded on the island for 12 days due to unfavorable weather, Mopsos tells Jason he must climb Mt. Dindymon and build an altar to Rhea.

There they found a massive vine stump, reared in the forest,

dead and dried out: this they cut away, to fashion

a sacred image of the mountain goddess, and Argos

carved it with elegance, and they set it up on that rugged      1120

summit, under the shade of the topmost oaks

that had taken root there, far above all the others.

Then they heaped up a gravel altar, hung it with garlands

of oak leaves, and offered up sacrifice, invoking

Dindyméné the mother, Lady of many names,      1125

dweller in Phrygia, and Títias and Kyllénos—

who alone are called fate-dispensers, and coadjutors

of the Idaian mother, out of that whole crowd

of Daktyls on Kretan Ida, long ago brought to birth

in Dikté's cave by the nymph Anchiálé, clutching      1130

fistfuls of earth from Oiaxos in either hand.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.1117–1131, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: 9. Feat to honor Rhea
features.note:
After building the altar to Rhea on Mt. Dindymon, the Argonauts hold a feast in her honor on Mt. Bear.

And then, on Bear Mountain, they made a feast to honor

the goddess, hymning Rhea, mistress of many names;

and at dawn the winds dropped, and they rowed on from the island. 

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.1150–1152, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: 10. Herakles (and Hylas) and Polyphémos are left behind
features.note:
A nymph falls in love with Herakles' squire, Hylas, and kidnaps him.

Hylas meanwhile, with bronze pitcher, had left his comrades

in search of some spring's hallowed flow,

[...]

Before her she saw young Hylas

in a blushing glow of sweet gracefulness and beauty:      1230

for on him the full moon, shining clear from heaven,

now cast its light. Aphrodite fluttered her senses,

[...] she at once

slipped her left arm round his neck from above, in urgent

longing to kiss his tender young mouth, and with her

right hand drew down his elbow, plunged him into mid-eddy.

Polyphémos goes to warn Herakles, who goes on a ramage searching for him. The rest of the Argonauts—without Herakles' leadership—accidentally leave them behind

[...] Herakles'

temples, and under his gut the black blood boiled.

In fury he threw down his fir trunk, and went sprinting

along the path, wherever his feet might take him in his haste.

[...]

and bellowing [...]

to shout, till the echoes rang, in that huge voice of his.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.1207–1277, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: 11. Conflict over leaving crew settled by Glaukos
features.note:
Sometime after they leave Kios they realize they left behind Herakles (and Hylas) and Polyphémos.

[...] then they

perceived that, all unknowing, they'd left those two ashore.

An argument breaks out and Télamon uses harsh words against Jason and he almost mutinies by lunging at Tiphys, when Boreas stops him.

Then Télamon, furious, shouted:

“Yes, sit there easy, small wonder, it suited you nicely      1290

to leave Herakles behind! This scheme was all your doing,

to stop his fame throughout Greece from eclipsing yours,

if it be that the gods grant us a safe homecoming!

But what's the point of talk? I'm going back, despite those

comrades of yours who planned this treachery with you.”      1295

So saying he sprang at Tiphys

Then a divine interpreter, Glaukos, appears out of the water and settles the argument by reassuring them it's ok to leave Herakles. 

“Why so determined, against great Zeus's counsels,      1315

to bring bold Herakles to Aiëtés' citadel?

In Argos his fate is to toil hard, for presumptuous

Eurystheus, fulfilling a total of twelve labors,

then to share hearth and home with the gods—if he accomplish

a few more still: so let him occasion no regrets. 

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.1284–1320, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: 12. End of Book I
features.note:
They arrive at a bend in the coastline (probably the head of the Gulf of Olbia) at sunrise.

All day and throughout the night a strong wind drove their

ship on her way; but as the dawn was breaking

a dead calm fell. Then, noting where a foreland

stood out from a curve in the coast, very widespread to the eye,

they bent to their oars, and landed there by sunrise.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.1358–1362, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Birthplace of Orpheus
features.note:
Birthplace of Orpheus (wikipedia), son of Oiágros and Kallíope.

First in our record be Orpheus, whom famous Kallíope,

after bedding Thracian Oiágros, bore, they tell us,

hard by Pimpleia's high rocky lookout: Orpheus,

who's said to have charmed unshiftable upland boulders

and the flow of rivers with the sound of his music.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.23–27, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Birthplace of Asteríon
features.note:
Birthplace of Asteríon, son of Kométes (mother not specified in Apollonius but in Apollodorus she's named Antigona)

Soon, too came Asteríon, begotten of Kométes

by Apídanos' turbulent waters, who had his dwelling

in Peirésiai of Thessalia, under a lofty mountain,

where mighty Apídanos and divine Enípeus

have their juncture, uniting in one from remote beginnings.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.35–39, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Birthplace of Polyphémos
features.note:
Birthplace of Polyphémos (wikipedia), son of Eílatos.

After them, leaving Lárissa, there followed that Polyphémos,

Eílatos's son, who once, among the sturdy Lapiths,

when the Lapiths were arming themselves against the Centaurs,

fought as a youth; though now his limbs were heavy

with age, his spirit remained a warrior's as always.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.40–44, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Birthplace of Iphiklos
features.note:
Birthplace of Iphiklos, son of King Phylacus and uncle to Jason on his mother's side, Alkimédé. He is from Phylaké in Pieria, but whose exact location is unknown.

Nor did Iphiklos tarry long in Phylaké, he being

Jason's uncle, Aison having married Alkimédé

of Phylaké: her kinship, that marriage bond, compelled him

to enroll himself in the company. 

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.45–48, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Birthplace of Admétos
features.note:
King of Phérai. (wikipedia)

[...] Nor did Admétos,

king over sheep-rich Phérai, hang back there under

the peaks of Thessalia's Chalkodónian mountains;

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.48–50, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Birthplace of son's of Hermes: Erytos, Echíon, and Aithálides
features.note:
Erytos and Echíon are skillful tricksters from Phthiótis and born to Antianeira, while Aithálides—also from Phthia—was born by the stream Amphryssos to Eupolemeia. 

nor did Hermes' two sons, Erytos and Echíon,

skillful tricksters both, rich in broad wheatfields,

stay behind in Phthiótis, while Aithálides, their third brother,

joined them on their departure. (Eupolemeia, fathered

by Myrmidon in Phthia, had him by the Amphryssos;

the other two Antianeira bore, Menétes' daughter.)

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.51–56, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Birthplace of Korónos
features.note:
Son of Kaineus, from "wealthy" Gyrton. (wikipedia)

There came too, leaving wealthy Gyrton, Korónos,

Kaineus's son, a brave man, yet not his father's equal:

for Kaineus, as singers tell, was among the living

still when destroyed by the Kentaurs: that day he drove them      60

back, alone of the heroes; and when they rallied

they could neither force him to yield, nor yet dispatch him,

but unbowed, unbroken, he went into earth down under,

crushed by a shattering hail of heavy pine trunks.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.57–64, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Birthplace of Mopsos
features.note:
His exact birthplace is not mentioned in the poem, but elsewhere it is said he's from Titaressa—location unknown—and that he was a Lapith. They are said to have occupied the Pineios river valley and Mt. Pelion. 

One of the two seers on the voyage.

Mopsos came too, the Thessalian, whom Apollo,      65

Leto's son, had made skilled in bird omens, above all mortals,

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.65–66, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Birthplace of Eurydamas
features.note:
Ktímenos' son, born in Dolopian Ktímené, by Lake Xynias. (wikipedia)

and Eurydamas, Ktímenos' son, who had his dwelling

in Dolopian Ktímené, by Lake Xynias.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.67–68, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Birthplace of Menoitios
features.note:
Son of Actor, from Opous.

[...] Actor

ordered forth his son Menoitios from Opous

to go with the flower of the heroes. 

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.68–70, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Birthplace of Jason
features.note:
Son Aison (wikipedia)

There's a land ringed with lofty mountains,      1085

teeming with sheep and cattle, where Prometheus,

Iápetos's scion, engendered noble Deukálion,

who was the first to build cities and raise up temples

to the immortal gods, first to be king among men:

and those dwelling along the marches call it Haimónia,      1090

and in it there lies Iolkos, my city

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 3.1085–1099, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Ausonia
features.note: (Italy) About Ausonia: trecani

features.name: Bosporos
features.note: Thrakian Bosporos (Kimmerian Bosporos is by Maiotic Lake)

features.name: Thrinákia
features.note: The ancient name for Sicily): sometimes Trinakria

features.name: Palléné
features.note:
[...] on they voyaged,

running before the wind, reaching by nightfall

the hills of Palléné, beyond Kanastron's headland. 

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.598–600, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Black Gulf
features.note:
Thence, moving briskly, they crossed the depths of the Black Gulf

with the Thrakian coast to port, and away to seaward

the island of Imbros. [924]

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.922–924, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Hellespontos
features.note:
Here they caught a stiff southerly wind and to the following

breeze bent their sail, thrust into the racing channel

of Athamas's daughter.

Athamas's daughter is a reference to the Hellenspont.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.926–928, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Krete
features.note: Home of King Minos.

features.name: Tauric Chersonesos
features.note: Crimea

features.name: Maiotic Lake
features.note: Sea of Azov

features.name: Mt. Ossa
features.note:
From there they glimpsed Eurymenai, and the sea-swept

ravines of Olympos and Ossa;

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.597–598, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Mt. Olympos
features.note:
From there they glimpsed Eurymenai, and the sea-swept

ravines of Olympos and Ossa;

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.597–598, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Imbros
features.note:
Thence, moving briskly, they crossed the depths of the Black Gulf

with the Thrakian coast to port, and away to seaward

the island of Imbros.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.922–924, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Samothrake
features.note:
Towards evening, at Orpheus's behest, they beached their vessel     

on the island of Atlas's daughter Elektra, that by learning

those secret rites, with their benign initiations,

they might steer in greater safety across the chilling deep [915–918]

features.name: Lemnos
features.note:
[...] with the last fading

rays of the sun, the wind dropped, and it was under oars

that they came to Sintian Lemnos's rocky shoreline.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.606–608, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Mt. Pelion
features.note:
On that day all the gods in heaven were spectators

of the ship and this race of demigods, valiantly steering

over the deep. On the topmost peaks of Pelion,

the nymphs gazed in amazement as they witnessed 550

Athena of Iton's handiwork, and the heroes themselves,

fists gripping and plying the oars.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.547–552, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Skithios
features.note:
and an ever-freshening breeze blew the vessel onward,

till Skiathos showed in mid-sea, and further distant,

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.579–583, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Cliffs of Pelion
features.note:
[...] Still pressing on, they sailed past the cliffs of

Pelion, left Cape Sepias below the horizon. 

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.581–582, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Mt. Athos
features.note:
Next day early, as they were sailing, the mass of Thrakian

Athos rose up before them. Though its distance from Lemnos

is as much as a well-found merchantman sails in a morning,

yet its highest peak casts a shadow as far as Myrína.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.601–604, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Mt. Ida
features.note:
They left the open sea behind them

at dawn and by nightfall were steering under the lee of

Rhoiteion's headland, with Ida firm on their starboard bow.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.927–929, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Kyzikós
features.note:
Within the Propontis there stands a beetling island,

just offshore from the fertile Phrygian domain,

sloping down to the sea, with sea-washed isthmus,

and sheer on the landward side. Its shores possess double

promontories. It lies north of the Aísepos River, 

and dwellers round about call it Bear Mountain.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.931–941, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Artákia
features.note:
It was here, too, in accordance with Tiphys's counsels,

that they dumped their small anchor stone, left it below a spring,

the spring of Artákia, chose another that suited them,

a massive one; but the first, by Apollo's oracles,

the Ionian Neleids afterwards consecrated,

very properly, in the shrine of Jasonian Athena.

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 1.955–960, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Thessaly
features.note:
Haimónia was Thessaly's ancient name even in the time period of the Argo

There's a land ringed with lofty mountains,

teeming with sheep and cattle, where Prometheus,

Iápetos's scion, engendered noble Deukálion,

who was the first to build cities and raise up temples

to the immortal gods, first to be king among men:

and those dwelling along the marches call it Haimónia,

(Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautika 3.1085–1090, trans. Peter Green, 2007)

features.name: Aborigines
features.note:
Once it was inhabited by savage and violent

aboriginals, an astonishing spectacle for their neighbors,

since each had six great powerful arms to brandish,

two springing from his stout shoulders, while the four

below were fitted to his monstrous rib cage. [942–946]

features.name: Doliones
features.note:
But the isthmus and plain were peopled by Doliónes,

fine men, over whom there ruled a hero, Aineios's son,

Kyzikós, whom the daughter of divine Eusóros,

Ainété, bore. [947–950]
